name: Vibravox
description: Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are also included in the corpus.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
publisher: Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés, Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, HESAM Université; French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL)
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, 'vibravox (revision 071945b),' 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created through a controlled recording protocol in which 200 participants (188 retained after post-processing) wore six audio sensors simultaneously. Each participant performed four recording steps: (1) reading sentences from French Wikipedia for 15 minutes in quiet conditions (speech-clean), (2) remaining silent in a noisy environment for 2 minutes 24 seconds (speechless-noisy), (3) remaining silent in complete silence for 54 seconds (speechless-clean), and (4) speaking in a noisy environment for 54 seconds (speech-noisy). Noise was rendered via a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers using a high-order ambisonics 3D spatializer. All six sensor signals were recorded simultaneously using a Zoom F8n field recorder at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution.
rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained after post-processing, with 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences excluded. Issues included mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, and instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped. In some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, automatic filters were not triggered.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Text for participant readings originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise samples were sourced from Audio Set (focused on battlefield and industrial noise classes) and in-house recordings of concerts and street events in 3rd and 5th order ambisonics. Audio was recorded simultaneously from six sensors: a headset microphone (Shure WH20XLR), a forehead accelerometer (Knowles BU23173-000), an in-ear soft foam microphone (Knowles FG-23329-P07), an in-ear rigid earpiece microphone (Knowles SPH1642HT5H), a throat microphone (iXradio XVTM822D-D35), and a temple vibration pickup (AKG C411).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel to attenuate low-frequency noise and artifacts. Voice Activity Detection (VAD) timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; in rare cases where adjusted timestamps exceeded original audio boundaries, audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The dataset was split by speaker with 80% in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test sets, ensuring no speaker overlap between splits.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-stage automatic filtering process was applied to the speech-clean subset. First, Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed using Levenshtein distance between labeled and Whisper-derived phonetic transcriptions; samples with PER > 10% were discarded. Second, a signal-to-noise ratio filter (SNR[i,j] = Lspeech_50[i,j] - Lsilence_50[i,j] > 1.5 dB) was applied to verify sensor functioning. Third, a sensitivity drift filter checked that Lspeech_50[i,j] > Lsilence_50[i] to detect sensor malfunctions. Only speech-clean samples passing all three filters were retained. All recordings for the other three subsets were included if the corresponding participant's speech-clean subset was not empty. Text normalization included lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes. Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the International Phonetic Alphabet via the CoML lab text phonemizer, with manual phonetic transcription for unrecognized words.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Textual transcriptions were sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice and filtered to remove proper names (except common first names, French town/region names, and country names), numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Phonetic transcriptions were generated automatically using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) with 33 French phonemes via the CoML lab text phonemizer. Manual phonetic transcription was performed for words not recognized by the phonemizer (e.g., 'algorithme'). Recording condition annotations (subset labels, sensor identifiers, split assignments) were also included.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: CoML lab text phonemizer (https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.03958); whisper-timestamped model (https://github.com/linto-ai/whisper-timestamped) for voice activity detection and phoneme error rate computation during post-processing
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed using the Levenshtein distance between labeled phonetic transcriptions and phonetic transcriptions derived from Whisper's output. Samples with PER > 10% were discarded to ensure high-quality labels. The whisper-timestamped model applied dynamic time warping to cross-attention weights to align transcriptions with raw waveforms for accurate word timestamp prediction.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available on HuggingFace under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. The dataset is versioned (revision 071945b referenced in the citation). A dedicated website is maintained at https://vibravox.cnam.fr/ with documentation and additional resources. Code is available at https://github.com/jhauret/vibravox.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains voice recordings of 188 participants. Age information is collected (mean age 28.55 years, range 18-82 years, with gender breakdown: females mean 25.9 years, males mean 31.4 years). Gender is recorded (97 female, 91 male speakers). The dataset is GDPR-compliant with informed consent obtained, data anonymized and encrypted during storage and analysis. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance research in body-conducted speech capture for robust communication in noisy environments, with applications in military operations, industrial settings, voice commands, and biometric authentication. The availability of French-language BCM data fills a gap in existing resources. The dataset could enable development of voice command systems, speaker verification for access control, and vital sign monitoring. Potential military applications include intelligence gathering and battlefield forensics.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is limited to French-language speech. The gender distribution is 97 female and 91 male speakers. Age distribution is skewed toward younger participants (median age 25 years overall). The noise recordings focus on battlefield and industrial environments, which may not represent all real-world acoustic scenarios. The Lombard effect (speakers increasing vocal effort in noisy conditions) means reported signal-to-external-noise ratios represent a lower bound on actual values. Some participants had ear canal anatomies that did not fit the rigid in-ear microphone properly, affecting acoustic sealing.
rai:dataLimitations: The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes as it lacks a clean reference under noisy conditions. The dataset contains only French speech, restricting direct applicability to other languages. Some sensors (particularly the temple vibration pickup) have very limited bandwidth, capturing signals only up to ~1500 Hz. The assumption that airborne and body-transmitted speech share a simple transfer function is inadequate for generating realistic synthetic data. Individual variance in sensor fit (especially in-ear microphones) affects recording quality. The manufacturing process for some novel sensors is not yet stabilized.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Validation, and Testing for: (1) Speech Enhancement / Bandwidth Extension - using speech-clean subset with airborne microphone as reference; (2) Speech-to-Phonemes / Automatic Speech Recognition - using transcribed speech-clean and speech-noisy subsets; (3) Speaker Verification - using speech-clean test subset with pretrained models; (4) Data augmentation by mixing speech-clean with speechless-noisy subsets to simulate noisy conditions; (5) Heart rate tracking and vital sign monitoring using speechless-clean subset; (6) Noise property analysis of body-conduction sensors; (7) Comparative analysis of different sensor technologies. The dataset is split 80/10/10 for train/validation/test by speaker.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each audio clip has: one text transcription, one phonetic transcription (IPA), and recording condition metadata (sensor type, subset, split assignment). For speech-clean, VAD timestamps are also provided per utterance.
rai:annotatorDemographics: 188 participants (97 female, 91 male). Age range: 18-82 years. Female mean age: 25.9 years, median: 22 years. Male mean age: 31.4 years, median: 27 years. Overall mean age: 28.55 years, median: 25 years. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group. All participants are residents/citizens subject to GDPR (European Union).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped (based on Whisper by OpenAI, with dynamic time warping for word-level timestamps) for voice activity detection and phoneme error rate computation; CoML lab text phonemizer for automatic IPA phonetic transcription; ambitools library for 3D audio spatialization of noise samples
